parent (such as messages) is read by the parent's ID once the parent has been
read within Bounds, and needs no rule of its own. Creates go through
`organizationFor`. `authz.Allows` says whether a permission is held at all, for
deciding what to show.

`GET /v1/permissions` serves the catalog to whoever builds roles, and
`authz.NormalizeGrants` and `authz.NormalizePermissions` check roles against it
on save.

Postgres enforces the organization boundary again underneath: see
[row-level security](row-level-security.md).

**Out of bounds looks like not found.** A record outside the caller's Bounds
is a `404`, so nobody can probe for another organization's records. Not
holding the permission at all is a `403`. The zero `Bounds` cover nothing, so
a query whose Bounds were never set finds nothing. A permission at a scope
that covers nothing, such as `team` while on no team, gets empty Bounds and not
an error.

**`authz.All`** is for the API's own lookups, such as re-reading something
just authorized under a lock. Every use in a service carries a comment saying
why. A permission neither kind of role can grant, such as `identity:sync`, is
held only by service actors.

**Stored roles.** Permissions and scopes are stored as text, so one removed
from the code simply stops counting. `api provision roles --apply` runs on
every deploy and makes sure Admin, Member, and Billing hold at least what
`authz.OrganizationRoles` gives them, so removing a permission from one of
those by hand lasts until the next deploy. A role any member holds, or marked
`assign_to_creator`, keeps `member:manage` (`ErrRoleManagesMembers`), so an
organization can't be left with nobody who can give it to anyone.

**Bootstrap.** On a new deployment nobody can manage roles.
`api access bootstrap --apply` makes someone the platform Administrator, and
every deploy runs it with `--create` for the platform's own administrator
(`.kube/migrate-job.yaml`).

**Adding to it.**

- **A permission** is a constant and `Definition` in `authz/catalog.go`,
  describing what each scope and the organization role give for it, and an
  `authz.Require` in the operations that need it. The catalog tests fail for a
  constant with no definition.
- **A platform scope** is a constant and its registry entry in
  `authz/scope.go`, which the scope tests fail without, offered on the
  permissions it applies to in the catalog. Data it needs about the caller
  comes through a method on `authz.Directory`, implemented in
  `internal/authn/directory.go`, which keeps `authz` free of the
  repositories. If it bounds records by something `authz.Bounds` doesn't hold,
  that's a field there and a condition in each bounds rule that honors it.
- **A resource** either has a bounds rule on its table, with `GetByID` taking
  `authz.Bounds` and its query a `Bounds` field, or is read only through a
  parent. Either way, its table needs row-level security.
- **A new place a request can act** isn't a new scope. Partnerships are the
  worked example: a route names it, `services.ReachPartnership` checks the
  caller belongs, and the request then runs on that place's own database role.
  A role table is only needed if admins must give its people different
  permissions.

mechanisms.name: Provider boundary
mechanisms.description: How the API reaches third-party services so that one can be swapped or stubbed without its callers noticing. Each service's own setup and behavior has a provider doc.
mechanisms.body:
Each type of provider is an interface in `internal/<type>`, with one
implementation per provider beneath it. An environment variable selects the
provider (the README's Configuration section lists them), and
`internal/bootstrap` builds it, refusing to start when the selected one is
missing a setting it requires. Payments, payouts, email, flags, and messaging
default to `noop` and storage to `memory`, so the local stack needs no third
party. Identity defaults to `clerk`, and has no stand-in.

In production, `.kube/configmap.yaml` selects each provider, and secrets are
GitHub secrets that `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` renders into
`.kube/secret.yaml`.

Every deploy's migrate Job (`.kube/migrate-job.yaml`) provisions what the code
defines, before the new pods start, and each step changes nothing when
everything is in step:

- `api migrate up`.
- `api provision payments stripe --apply`, for the capacity types' products
  and prices.
- `api provision roles --apply`, for the organization roles.
- `api access bootstrap --create --apply`, for the platform's own
  administrator.

Everything else in a provider doc's Setup is done by hand, and stays that way.

Each provider that reaches an external service has a check on
`GET /v1/healthz`, run every 30 seconds in the background. Noop, memory, and
local providers have none.

`/v1/readyz` leaves the providers out, so an outage at one never takes the API
out of rotation. Bootstrap checks only that settings are present. Nothing at
start-up checks that a key works, or that a domain or bucket is right: those
show up as failures when they're used.

**Adding a payments provider** needs, without changing the API's contract or
the front end:

- An implementation of `payments.Provider` (`internal/payments/provider.go`) in
  `internal/payments/<provider>`. Its package doc lists what a provider must
  support: hosted pages for payment methods, billing details, invoices and each
  invoice, charging a saved default off-session at once, working out, quoting,
  and collecting each invoice's tax, idempotency keys kept for at least 24
  hours, and statuses mapped onto the API's. A provider that can't work out tax
  calls a tax service from inside its own implementation. Callers only ever
  get the addresses of the provider's pages, and each `page` names what the
  client is doing.
- A webhook handler, with its own signature check and route, that calls
  `InvoiceService.Sync` when one of its invoices changes.
- Its settings in `internal/config` and `internal/bootstrap`, the README's
  variables, and a provider doc.

A provider with no hosted pages for payment methods, only an embedded card
form, doesn't fit: it would need payment method screens of our own.

mechanisms.name: Row-level security
mechanisms.description: Postgres enforces the organization and partnership boundaries underneath the application's Bounds, so a query that forgets its Bounds still can't cross them in a request acting in an organization or a partnership.
mechanisms.body:
Every table holding an organization's records has an `organization_id`, filled
from its parent by a trigger, with row-level security forced. Every table with
a partnership's records that a request acting in one reaches has a
`partnership_id`, or is `partnerships` itself, the same way.

| Role | Connection | Used by | Reaches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_organization` | `DATABASE_ORGANIZATION_URL` | A request acting in an organization | That organization's rows, and shared tables as granted |
| `api_partner` | `DATABASE_PARTNER_URL` | A request acting in a partnership, as its manager | That partnership's rows. No organization's, and no shared table |
| `api_platform` | `DATABASE_PLATFORM_URL` | Staff, service actors, webhooks, the command line, and authentication | Every row. Bounds are all that limit it |
| The owner | `DATABASE_URL` | Migrations and `api provision database` | Everything; it skips row-level security |

The connection is picked in one place, `conn.exec`, from
`repositories.ScopeOf(ctx)`: the organization the Principal acts in, unless a
service has set another scope. On `api_organization`, every statement runs in a
transaction that sets `app.organization_id` with `SET LOCAL`: a `UnitOfWork`'s,
or a short one of its own. `api_partner` sets `app.partnership_id` the same
way. A statement with none set errors instead of returning rows.

**Acting in a partnership.** No header names one. A route with one in its path
reaches it through `services.ReachPartnership`, which reads who manages it on
`api_platform` and, for its manager, returns
`repositories.InPartnership(ctx, id)`. Everything after runs on `api_partner`,
except reading the partnership's clients (below). Admins holding
`partner:manage` stay on `api_platform`, as they do for organizations.

**Reaching across organizations.** A few things a request acting in an
organization does aren't that organization's. A service asks for them with
`repositories.AcrossOrganizations(ctx)`, which only changes the connection, so
Bounds still apply. Use it only for what really is shared: what belongs to the
person calling (the organizations they're in, creating another, their
invitations), and what's shared by every client (how full a week is, as a
total naming nobody).

**What a partner's connection doesn't reach.** `api_partner` reaches no
`users`, so a service reads people before it acts in the partnership. It
reaches no `organizations` either, so a manager's list of their partnership's
clients, which needs the clients' names, reads `partnership_clients` on
`api_platform` once `ReachPartnership` has allowed it
(`PartnershipClientService.List`). Only the query's `partnership_id` filter
keeps it to that partnership, and the policy does nothing there, so the filter
stays, and what it returns of a client is only its name. The other way round,
a client's people read the name of the partnership that referred it the same
way (`PartnershipClientService.ReferredBy`), keyed by their organization.

**Limited tokens.** A token limited to some organizations doesn't widen
through `AcrossOrganizations`: anything reading that way on the caller's
behalf honors `Principal.Limited()`.

**Policies.** Each role's policies name only that role. A table holding both
kinds of rows, such as `agreements`, has an `organization_isolation` policy for
`api_organization` and a `partnership_isolation` one for `api_partner`, and
neither evaluates the other's setting. `payout_recipients` holds people's and
partnerships' recipients. It's in `sharedTables`, as it has no
`organization_id`, but has row-level security: `api_partner` reaches only its
partnership's, `api_organization` only people's, and `api_platform` every one.
Nothing but the service's lookup by the caller keeps one person from
another's.

**Credentials.** The server refuses to start if any of the first three
connects as anyone else, or as a superuser or a role with `BYPASSRLS`. The
owner must be a superuser, or have `BYPASSRLS` and `CREATEROLE`. Only the
`migrate` Job has the owner's credential, not the API's pods (see
`.kube/secret.yaml`). Changing a password takes down any pod still using it.

**Adding a table** means deciding if it's an organization's, a partnership's,
or shared:

- **An organization's** has an `organization_id`, a trigger or a value for it,
  row-level security, both policies, and grants to `api_organization`.
- **A partnership's** is listed in `partnershipTables` in the partnership
  integration test. If a request acting in the partnership needs it, it has a
  `partnership_id`, row-level security, a `partnership_isolation` policy for
  `api_partner`, a `platform_access` one, and grants to `api_partner`.
- **A shared one** is listed in `sharedTables` in the integration test.

The integration tests fail for a table that's none of these.
`api_organization` and `api_partner` get nothing on a new table until a
migration grants it, and `api_platform` gets it by default.

mechanisms.name: Telemetry
mechanisms.description: What the API emits and how to read it. The API exports over OTLP to the collector `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` names, which in the cluster is the Grafana Alloy collector the exalynt/collector repo deploys, forwarding to Grafana Cloud. The README's Configuration section covers the settings.
mechanisms.body:
Every request gets a SERVER span named for its route template, with a CLIENT
span per query under it, such as `SELECT estimates`, and one per call to a
provider. Each log line carries `trace_id` and `span_id`, there's one per
request, and a 5xx logs the error behind it.

Each feature has a `<feature>.changes` counter, by `operation` and `outcome`.
Reading the names from the code is quickest: search for `Int64Counter(`.

Queries' spans carry their text but never their values, and invitees' email
addresses are never logged.

**Reading it.**

- A counter's `failure` includes a caller's mistake, such as a `404`, a `409`,
  or a full week. The request spans say which.
- Assigning a new client that finds no team counts as a `success` on
  `teams.changes`. The `POST /v1/organizations` span has a `team not assigned`
  event saying why.
- A slow request with fast queries is waiting on a provider, which its CLIENT
  spans show.
- A `SELECT` waiting a long time on `users` or `capacities` means lock
  contention on an engineer, a block, or a week.

**Exporting.** `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`'s port matches
`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL`: the collector's HTTP port (4318) for
`http/protobuf`, the default, or its gRPC port (4317) for `grpc`. A mismatch
fails every export, and only the warnings on stderr say so.

components.name: Access tokens
components.description: Personal access tokens, which identify their creator to the API without a session. How one becomes a caller is in the [authentication doc](../mechanisms/authentication.md).
components.body:
Only the secret's SHA-256 is kept, unsalted on purpose: 256 random bits need no
salt or slow hash, and a request has to find its token by it. The secret can't
be shown again, so a token revoked by mistake can only be replaced. Revoking
deletes the row, and a revoked token is simply unknown.

A banned user's tokens are refused, not deleted, as Clerk ending someone's
sessions doesn't reach a token. `users.banned` follows Clerk's `banned` from
the `user.updated` webhook and `api sync users clerk`, and lifting the ban
makes the tokens work again. A lockout from failed sign-ins is short-lived and
doesn't count.

`organization_ids` is NULL for a token with no limit. It's IDs in a column and
not rows with foreign keys, so nothing can empty the list and make a limited
token look unlimited. Membership is still checked each request, so someone
leaving an organization stops the token working there, and rejoining restores
it.

Anything that reads with `AcrossOrganizations` on the caller's behalf honors
`Principal.Limited()`, as `GET /v1/users/me` and `GET /v1/organizations` do.
`POST /v1/organizations`, the caller's invitations, and
`/v1/users/me/payout-account` refuse a limited token instead.

`access_tokens` has no row-level security, as a token belongs to a person and
not an organization. The `user_id` in each query is what keeps people apart.

A refused token's span says why in `auth.access_token.refusal`, as the caller
is only told it was refused. Spans carry `auth.method`, and a token's has
`auth.access_token.id`.

`last_used_at` changes at most once a minute, but the `UPDATE` is still sent
on each request. Failing to record it doesn't fail the request.

components.name: Agreements
components.description: Client, Engineer and Partner Agreements: rendered from versioned templates, offered to a party, accepted, and kept as the PDF made when accepted.
components.body:
An offer is a row with its type, version and Commercial Terms. While it's
offered, its document is rendered on every read, filled in with the party as
they are now. Accepting renders it once more, lays it out as a PDF in Go, puts
the PDF in object storage under a key of its own, then records the row as
accepted. If recording fails, the PDF is deleted again, as best it can be. The
accepted row keeps the party's name as the document named it, and the PDF is
never rendered again. Earnings read the terms of the latest accepted Engineer
Agreement (`InEffectTerms`).

**Who reads which agreements.** Engineers' agreements belong to no
organization, so they're read on the platform connection
(`AcrossOrganizations`), where row-level security lets everything through.
Only the service's party filter keeps one person from another's: nothing lists
or gets without a party in the `AgreementQuery`, and an `AgreementQuery`
naming none matches nothing. An organization's are read on the organization
connection, where row-level security keeps them apart too. A partnership's are
read by its manager on the partner connection, where row-level security keeps
partnerships apart, but by an admin holding `partner:manage` on the platform
connection (`ReachPartnership`), where only `partnerParty`'s filter does.

**One offer per party and type** is held by `DeleteOffered` and a partial
unique index. Two admins sending at the same moment means one gets a `500`
from the index, and sends again.

**Deleting a user.** A user's offers are deleted by
`UserService.DeleteByIdentity` before the user, since only accepted rows may be
left with no party. Deleting a user any other way, such as a test's cleanup,
deletes their agreements first or leaves rows behind.

**Templates.** A template version that anyone has accepted never changes: the
next version is added instead. Shared definitions in `definitions.go` are
pulled into every version that uses them, so editing one rewrites every
waiting offer, though not accepted PDFs.

**Deleting an organization or partnership.** `agreements.organization_id` is
`ON DELETE CASCADE` (migration 76), so deleting an organization would delete
its accepted Client Agreements and leave their PDFs behind. Nothing deletes an
organization today; whatever first does decides what happens to them.
`agreements.partnership_id` cascades the same way: today only revoking a
partner's invitation deletes a partnership, and only before its agreement can
be accepted.

The `agreements/` keys in object storage are the only copy of what was
accepted.

components.name: Availability
components.description: How much of a week each engineer offers, which Capacity adds up per team.
components.body:
An engineer has rows in `availabilities`, each a weekly RFC 5545 recurrence
rule and not a row per week:

| Kind | Rule | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `baseline` | `FREQ=WEEKLY` | What they offer each week from `starts_on`. One each, by a partial unique index |
| `override` | `FREQ=WEEKLY;COUNT=n` | Replaces it for n weeks, at most 52. Never two for one week |
| `past_baseline` | `FREQ=WEEKLY;COUNT=n` | What the baseline offered before it last changed. Never shown or changed |

A week resolves to the override covering it, otherwise the baseline or past
baseline covering it, otherwise 0. `AvailabilityService.Weeks` does that for
one engineer and `CapacityService.totalUnits` for many, both through
`applyWeeks`.

**Past weeks** are protected in the service and not just the page. A baseline
already under way that changes leaves a `past_baseline` for its weeks so far,
and its `starts_on` moves up. The seeders and tests' setup write earlier rows
through the repository, which doesn't know about any of this.

**Locking.** Every change first locks the engineer's `users` row
(`AvailabilityRepository.LockUser`), so overlap checks hold. Setting a first
baseline doesn't need it, as the unique index allows only one.

**Taking blocks out.** Every change runs through `AvailabilityService.change`,
which compares the engineer's weeks before and after in the same transaction
and has `CapacityService.fitEngineerWeeks` (`room_fitting.go`) take blocks out
of the ones that went down. A dry run makes the change and rolls it back.
Scheduling and claiming read availability without the engineer's lock; the
week locks fitting takes serialize them.

**A run of weeks at once.** `POST /availability/{id}/changes` sets a run of
weeks in one transaction, replacing the overrides that cover them. The console
used to do that with several calls, which passed through weeks briefly back at
the baseline: with blocks taken out on every reduction, that would take out
blocks the final state still fits.

**Who reaches it.** `availabilities` is shared and holds no client's data, so
row-level security doesn't apply. `api_organization` can only read it, for
Capacity's room, and clients see only totals. `availability:manage` only ever
reaches the caller's own: an admin can set their own and not an engineer's.

`GET /v1/users/{id}/availability` isn't paged. Its window is capped at 53
weeks, which acts as its page size.

components.name: Billing
components.description: How the API charges for capacity through a payment provider. Clients handle payment methods, billing details, and invoices on the provider's own pages. How a provider plugs in is in the [provider boundary doc](../mechanisms/provider-boundary.md).
components.body:
The API keeps only the organization's customer with the provider, and an
`invoices` row: `provider`, `external_id`, `status`, and the purchase's
`idempotency_key`. Each block points at its invoice, which is how a webhook
finds the blocks an invoice settles, and how a retry finds what it bought.

`POST /v1/billing-sessions` sends a client to the provider. Its `page` names
what the client is doing, never one of the provider's pages, and the provider
opens what it has. `GET /v1/invoices/{id}` reads everything but the row from
the provider each time. Provider links to an invoice's page expire, so they're
read when opened and never stored.

A billing session's URL is a short-lived credential for the organization's
billing. It's never cached or logged, and its return address comes from
`APP_URL`, never the request.

**A purchase** asks the provider for the default, charges it on an invoice of
its own, and only then records the invoice and blocks. The provider works out
the tax on it and adds it; `GET /v1/capacity-quote` asks it for the same
invoice's totals without charging, and a purchase sent with that total as
`quoted_total_cents` is refused if the provider's total differs.

- The charge happens before the invoice is written, and webhooks for an
  invoice the API has no record of are acknowledged and ignored. The log line
  says "charged but not recorded on invoice".
- Retrying with the same `Idempotency-Key` records the blocks without charging
  again, for as long as the provider keeps the key, at least 24 hours.
- A default deleted between the check and the charge reads as a decline: the
  invoice is voided and nothing is owed.
- Provider calls happen while the organization's row is locked, so each has a
  timeout. With Stripe that's 10 seconds, retried twice on a network error, so
  half a minute at most.

**Later status changes** come from the provider's webhook, or
`api sync invoices`, each reading the provider's current state in a
transaction that locks the organization's row.

- A webhook redelivered or out of order is safe, as it always reads current
  state. A failed write catches up on the next webhook or `api sync invoices`.
- `api sync invoices` only compares statuses, and only walks invoices the API
  recorded.
- The webhook acts as the API itself (`billing:sync`), and only on the invoice
  its event names.

components.name: Capacity
components.description: Blocks of engineering capacity: bought, scheduled into a week, staffed, started, and fulfilled, each with at most one focus.
components.body:
A block moves `pending` → `available` → `scheduled` → `in_progress` →
`fulfilled`, and back from `scheduled` to `available` when it's unscheduled
before its week starts. `CapacityService.Start` moves it to `in_progress` and
`FulfillmentService.Fulfill` to `fulfilled`, setting `fulfilled_at` and earning
its shares in the same transaction.

A client's room in a week comes only from the engineers on teams assigned to
it. `GET /v1/capacity-weeks` reports it and scheduling checks it: what those
engineers offer, the client's own scheduled blocks, and other clients' blocks
taking from the same engineers. `GET /v1/capacity-weeks` reads across
organizations and returns only totals.

When an engineer's availability goes down, `fitWeeks` in `room_fitting.go`
takes blocks out of each week it went down in: the engineer's own blocks by
`staffed_at` (`pickToFree`), then blocks nobody's on by `scheduled_at`
(`pickToFit`). Whether those fit is a maximum flow from each client's blocks to
what the engineers on its teams have left, so a client with two teams isn't
counted in full against each. It covers only the clients linked to the
engineer's team through shared clients. `api capacity fit-weeks` runs the same
over every engineer and client, for weeks overbooked some other way.

**Locking.** Everything that changes a block reads it `FOR UPDATE` first,
including settling an invoice. Scheduling and claiming also take the same
advisory lock on the week before checking its room. The order is always row
lock first, then week lock. Fitting locks every block booked in the weeks it
covers, then the weeks, then lists again, so it keeps the row-then-week order
and still sees blocks scheduled in between. Block numbers come from a counter
on the organization's row, which that row's lock serializes.

**Fitting and scheduling disagree at the edges.**

- Fitting only unschedules blocks nobody's on, and only one whose removal
  makes the shortfall smaller. Blocks whose engineer is on no team count only
  against that engineer. What's still short after that is left, which a
  reduction then refuses.
- Scheduling still checks a client's room by `clientRoom`, which counts
  another client's open blocks in full, so it can refuse a week fitting would
  call room enough.
- The claim preview (`ClaimPreview`) takes no locks, and asks whether one
  engineer alone could take each other block, not whether the combined room
  covers it as scheduling does. So it can warn of a block
  `GET /v1/capacity-weeks` counts as fitting, and a claim made just after can
  strand a block it didn't name.

**Moving and unscheduling.** Moving a block takes any engineer off it, without
working out whether they fit the new week. Unscheduling one does too, and
takes no week lock, as freeing room can't overbook it. `scheduled_at` and
`staffed_at` are set by `Capacity.SetWeek` and `SetEngineer`, not the
repository, and anything writing a block's week or engineer goes through them,
or the latest-first order is wrong. Blocks booked before the column was added
took `updated_at` as their guess.

**Starting and fulfilling.** `Start` is gated by `capacity:manage`, so a lead
or admin who can manage a block can start it too, while `Fulfill` checks that
the caller is the block's engineer and no permission does. `Start` answers
forbidden, not not found, to someone who can read the block but not manage it,
and refuses before `WeekStart`, Monday in UTC. A fulfilled block can have no
`fulfilled_at`: one fulfilled before review existed has none. Migration 00087
dropped `capacity_review_events` and can't be undone, so code from before it
can't run against a database past it. Going back means restoring reviews from
a backup.

**Focuses.** The repository fills `Capacity.Focus` on every read of blocks, a
get or a list, with one more query, so anything reading blocks pays for it.
The rest of focuses is in [focuses](focuses.md).

**Purchases.** A purchase carries on if the caller goes away, so closing the
page can't leave a charge unrecorded. What the charge does is in the
[billing doc](billing.md). `Idempotency-Key` is stored on the invoice and sent
to the provider on each step. A repeat answers with what was bought, records
what was charged but not recorded, or is a `409` if the first is under way,
differs, or was voided. The portal keeps the key while the outcome is unknown,
and makes a new one when the choices change.

**Admins and claiming.** A caller acting in no organization, such as an admin,
sees every engineer's availability and every booking. That's what the admin's
overbooked-weeks note reads, so it only catches Exalynt-wide overbooking. Any
platform role other than Administrator needs `capacity:claim` granted at team
scope on the Roles page. Administrator holds `capacity:claim` at team scope,
the only scope it offers, so an admin claims only for clients their team
supports.

components.name: Earnings
components.description: What engineers, leads, and partnerships earn on fulfilled blocks, recorded as each is fulfilled.
components.body:
An earning has exactly one payee, `user_id` or `partnership_id`, which
`earnings_one_payee` enforces. A referral earning's `UserID` is `uuid.Nil` in
the model, so earnings are grouped or filtered by payee type, never by
`UserID` alone.

**Which partnership a block earns for** is `capacities.partnership_id`, set by
`CapacityService.Create` from the attribution at purchase and never updated.
It isn't worked out from `partnership_clients`, which only says where the
client is attributed now. Migration 00094 filled it in for blocks bought
before it, but only those bought since their client was attributed.

**The earning window** has no column of its own: it opens at the earliest of
the client's blocks with that `partnership_id`. Deleting a block, as voiding
its invoice does, can move it.

**A partnership's earnings** are read on the platform connection once
`ReachPartnership` has let the caller in, as its clients' blocks and names are
theirs, and `api_partner` reaches no organization's rows. They're paged a block
at a time (`PagePartnership`): each of its blocks but pending ones, with its
referral earning, or with none for the service to work out what it would pay.
A block bought after its client's window closed pays nothing and is dropped
after the query, so a page can be short. The terms are read once and the
windows once a page, rather than calling `referralShare` per block.

`PagePartnership` doesn't read the block's engineer, and the resource never
shows one on a referral earning: partners aren't told who worked a block.

The `Earning` resource, `EarningRepository` and
`GET /partnerships/{id}/earnings` are shared with partner earnings, which is
Beta, so they hold to Beta even though a person's earnings is Alpha.

components.name: Estimates
components.description: An estimate and everything in it is one document, replaced whole.
components.body:
`PUT /v1/estimates/{id}` replaces the estimate in one transaction: it updates
the `estimates` row first, which locks it, then deletes its discounts and
Focuses, which cascades to their notes, and inserts the new ones. Focuses,
notes, and discounts keep the IDs a request sends and get new UUIDv7s where it
leaves them out, so the console can keep its React keys from the first
keystroke.

`Replace` and `Delete` repeat the caller's bounds in their `WHERE`, against the
row as it stands once locked, so an estimate moved out of someone's team while
they were saving it isn't written over.

`focus_count` and `units_*` are denormalized by `Estimate.RecountTotals` in the
same transaction, so a listing needn't add up Focuses. Costs aren't stored. A
listing carries each estimate's Focuses in brief and discounts in full, each
loaded for the whole page in one extra query.

The console does the discount arithmetic too, so a change lands in both:
`price - (price × total + 50) / 100` in whole cents.

`include_operations` and `operations_fee_cents` stay in the API though the UI
doesn't show operations for now, and a save from the editor leaves the flag as
it was.

A Focus's pace is `estimate_focuses.capacity`; one written without it is
planned at Dedicated.

components.name: Focuses
components.description: A block's focus: what its work is about, with images, videos, and files from its organization's objects.
components.body:
A focus is its own row in `focuses`, with `focus_attachments`, and blocks point
at it by `capacities.focus_id`, which several blocks can share.
`FocusService.Use` keeps them to the focus's own organization; nothing in the
schema does.

**Who may change a focus** follows `focusBounds`
(`internal/services/capacity_reach.go`) on any block it's on:
`capacity:manage` for Exalynt's people, or, since that's platform-only,
`focus:manage`, which only an organization role grants, for the client's own
blocks. `Update` locks every such block. A focus on no block has no block to
check, so `FocusService` treats it as not found for changes, while it can still
be read and put back on a block.

`GET /focuses` checks those bounds reaching the organization, or else lists the
caller's blocks of that organization to see they manage one. That list is
unpaginated, fine for an engineer's own blocks.

**Row-level security.** `focuses` and `focus_attachments` are
organization-scoped with row-level security, and `api_organization` may insert
and update focuses and insert and delete their attachments, never delete a
focus. Its policies keep a client to its own. An attachment row carries its
own `organization_id` for its policy, which `checkAttachments`
(`internal/services/attachments.go`, shared with
[work updates](work-updates.md)) keeps equal to its focus's by refusing another
organization's object.

components.name: Organizations
components.description: Client organizations, their members, invitations, payment customer, and logo.
components.body:
Who made each change is the `user_id` on its request's log line, and `user.id`
on its span: there's no audit table. Closing an account is done by hand, by the
close-an-organization runbook, and the organization routes' alert links the
respond-to-organization-errors runbook.

Security was reviewed on 2026-11-19, for GA, by reading the code: routes and
permissions, invitation acceptance, row-level security, logos, email, logs,
and sign-up. It led to the daily invitation cap per person as well as per
organization, treating a primary address Clerk marks unverified as none, and a
sign-in redirect that can't name another host. What it accepted is the
`member:manage` tradeoff in [authorization](../mechanisms/authorization.md).

**Invitations.** The daily invitation cap counts
`organization_invitation_sends`, not invitations, which are deleted when
accepted or revoked. It counts the organization's sends or the inviter's,
across organizations, so it's read across organizations before the
transaction, unlocked: invitations sent at the same moment can go a few over.
An invitation is saved and its email sent in one transaction, so a failing
email provider fails the request with `500` and nothing is saved.

**Creating one.** `POST /organizations` with an `Idempotency-Key` returns the
organization the caller first created with it (`organization_creation_keys`,
keyed by user and key), whatever name the retry sends. A retry that races the
first request waits on the key's unique index, then returns the first's
organization.

**The last manager.** The last-manager check locks the organization's row
(`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`), so two changes at once can't each count on the other
member to remain.

**The payment customer.** `EnsurePaymentsCustomer` runs when someone goes to
manage billing, not at sign-up, so its failures show on
`POST /v1/billing-sessions` and not on these routes. It calls the provider
while holding the organization's row, with a 10-second timeout, so a slow
provider fails the request instead of holding every other change to the
organization.

- Creating a customer is idempotent: it looks by the ID on record, then by the
  organization's ID in metadata, and carries an idempotency key. If the
  database write fails after the provider created one, the next call finds
  it.
- Nothing overwrites a customer's details afterward, including renaming the
  organization, so invoices keep the name the client gave the provider.

**Logos.** A logo's bytes are stored first under a new key, then the row
points at them under the lock, and the old bytes are deleted at once. A failed
delete strands bytes with nothing pointing to them, which costs nothing for a
reader.

components.name: Partnerships
components.description: Partnerships and what their managers do in them: invite clients, see the clients attributed to them, and accept their Partner Agreements. How a request acts in one is in the [row-level security doc](../mechanisms/row-level-security.md), and Partner Agreements themselves are in [agreements](agreements.md).
components.body:
**Earning windows.** A client's earning window on the clients list comes from
`EarningService.Windows`, one query for the page's clients
(`CapacityRepository.FirstBoughtFor`), and a partnership's earnings use the
same `windows`, so how a window opens changes in one place, or the list and
what's paid disagree.

**Revoked invitations.** Every read of `client_invitations` but
`CountInvitationsSince` leaves out revoked rows, as does the unique index on an
address, so a revoked address can be invited again. A new query does the same.

**How a client came.** `findReferral` records `invitation` rather than
`referral_code` when the code's partnership has a pending invitation to the
creator's address, since the invitation email's link carries the code.
Attributions made before that kept `referral_code`, so older clients who came
by invitation still read as by code.

**Who referred a client.** A client's people read who referred it through
`PartnershipClientService.ReferredBy` (`GET /organizations/{id}/referral`), on
`api_platform` once `requireOrganization` has allowed it, as no organization's
connection reaches `partnership_clients` or `partnerships`. Only its
`organization_id` key keeps it to that client, and what it returns is kept to
the partnership's name.

`ListClients` and `ListInvitations` stay unpaged for the platform's own lookups
(the admin list, attribution by address); the partner's listings go through
`PageClients` and `PageInvitations`.

components.name: Payouts
components.description: How earnings become money sent, to people and to partnerships.
components.body:
**Never sent twice.**

- A payout is saved before the provider is asked to send it, so its ID can be
  the idempotency key. A crash in between would otherwise leave money sent
  with no record of it, so the order stays.
- Only an error that means nothing was sent lets a payout's earnings go. Any
  other error from the provider leaves it Processing with no external ID, and
  the next release sends it again under the same ID. Marking one of those
  Failed would pay someone twice.
- `payout_earnings.active` is what stops an earning being sent twice, through a
  partial unique index. It's false once a payout has failed or been canceled,
  which is what puts the earning back in the next release.
- A webhook can arrive before the release has saved the provider's ID, and
  it's acknowledged and ignored. The next event for that payout puts it right.

**What a payout keeps.** A payout's lines copy the figures they had, and their
foreign keys don't cascade, because what a sent payout lists must survive
changes to blocks, people, and clients.

**Who reaches it.** `payouts` has no row-level security and only the platform
role can reach it. `PayoutService` always acts across organizations.

**Payees.** A payee is a person or a partnership, and the same ID could in
principle be either, so a release groups earnings by payee type and ID, and a
payout listing filters on `payee_type` as well as `payee_id`.

**Shared with partner payouts.** The release, `send`, the payouts tables and
the `Payout` resource are shared with partner payouts, which is Beta, so they
hold to Beta even though the admin and console sides are Alpha: they change
without breaking it, and schema is added with new migrations. A partnership's
payouts are paged (`PagePayee`), but a person's and the admin's list still
load whole through `List`.

**Payouts from before Stripe Connect.** Payouts released on the `noop`
provider before production moved to Stripe Connect are kept, `provider` =
`noop`, Paid with no money moved. That was decided, and they aren't treated as
sent when reconciling with Stripe. Migration 98 cleared the `noop` recipients.

components.name: Spaces
components.description: Our records of each organization's conversation space and who we put in it, kept in step with the messaging provider as memberships change, and blocks' conversations there. The provider is behind messaging: Google Chat or Stream.
components.body:
For spaces and memberships our row comes first and the provider follows. Its
`provider` and `provider_id` stay null until the provider has the thing, and a
record naming another provider counts as not made yet.

- **A space** is recorded in `OrganizationService.CreateReferred`'s
  transaction, with the organization.
- **A block's conversation** is the other way round: `StartBlockConversation`
  has the provider start it within the request, making the space with the
  provider first if it isn't yet, and records it only once that worked, with
  no transaction around the call. A failure records nothing and is the
  caller's error (502), so they can try again.
- **The membership changes with the provider** run after the change commits.
  The services whose changes affect who belongs call one `Spaces` method each:
  - `OrganizationService`: creating an organization, removing a member.
  - `InvitationService`: accepting an invitation to an organization or the
    platform.
  - `TeamService`: assigning and unassigning a client, putting someone on a
    team, taking them off, deleting a team.
  - `RoleService`: taking a platform role away.
  - `UserService`: banning a user, deleting a user.

  Each service gets the hook through `SpacesWith`, wired in `serve`.
- **Every method is the happy path for one change.** It skips what's already
  done, records failures on the request's span, and never fails the change.
- **Whatever a change unlinks is read before it**, such as a team's clients
  before the team is deleted.

`spaces` and `space_memberships` are api_platform's only: no grant opens them
to the organization or partner roles. A block's conversations are for its
client too, so `SpaceService` checks `capacity:read` reaches the block's
organization itself and then reads and writes across organizations, since it
needs the space.

**Without the hook.** A hook that isn't wired is skipped silently: tests and
the CLIs build services without one. An organization created straight through
the repository, as test fixtures are, has no space, so starting a conversation
on its blocks is refused; the acceptance tests make Acme's and Globex's spaces
themselves. Deleting a user without the hook still deletes their memberships
by cascade, but leaves them in the provider's spaces.

**Two at once.** Two people starting a conversation on the same subject at
once both reach the provider before the unique index refuses the second, which
leaves its thread with the provider and no record of it.

**The noop provider** takes any space or conversation it's asked about as
existing, since it forgets everything on restart, so records it made earlier
still work locally.

**Deleting an organization** leaves its space behind, since a space stands on
its own. Acceptance tests and the seeders' reset leave such spaces in the
local database.

components.name: Teams
components.description: Who at Exalynt a client sees and, through the `team` scope, which clients' records an engineer can reach.
components.body:
`teams`, `team_members` (keyed by user, so the one-team rule is the primary
key), and `team_clients`. A partial unique index keeps one lead per team, and
a unique index on `lower(name)` holds names distinct.

`OrganizationService.Create` assigns a new client a team once its organization
exists, through `CapacityService.AssignLeastLoadedTeam`: fewest unfulfilled
units, then fewest clients, then first by name, among teams with an engineer
offering time in one of the next three weeks. Assigning runs outside the
sign-up's transaction so it can't undo the sign-up, and always as the system,
not the person signing up. When no team qualifies, the client signs up with
none.

**Members.** Someone who loses their platform role keeps their row on the team
but isn't read as a member, so giving a role back restores them. A team's row
is locked while someone's put on it, so two people made its lead at once take
turns.

**Releasing blocks.** Changing a team's members or clients, or deleting it,
also runs `CapacityService.ReleaseIneligible` in the same transaction, across
organizations, which takes engineers off upcoming blocks of clients they no
longer support. That's wired with `TeamService.ReleaseBlocksWith` in `serve`;
a `TeamService` built without it, as in unit tests, leaves blocks alone. It
locks every upcoming block, which is fine at a few hundred.

**Reads.** A client's teams and a person's team are read unpaginated inside
the API, the second on each request an engineer makes with a `team` grant.
Both are a few rows. Of a team's clients a caller sees only those they reach,
so a client never learns who else a team works with. A list's cursor holds
only its place, so following another caller's reads only the caller's own
teams.

components.name: Work updates
components.description: What engineers write about a block's work as they do it, shown on its page with when it was started and fulfilled.
components.body:
**Blocks and focuses.** `work_updates.capacity_id` and `focus_id` are both
nullable, so an update can be about a focus alone, but no CHECK requires one
of them: `WorkUpdateService` always sets the block. Nothing posts or lists
focus-only updates yet, and `writers` treats one as not found. Adding them
means deciding whose permission reaches a focus on no block. Updates are
listed by `capacity_id` only, so an update stays on the block it was posted on
even after the block's focus changes, and the focus it was about is only its
`focus_id`.

**Who writes.** `work_updates` and `work_update_attachments` are
organization-scoped with row-level security, and `api_organization` has
`SELECT` only. Only a request acting in no organization writes one.

**Deleting** keeps the row: `Delete` empties text, metrics, links, and
attachments and sets `deleted_at`. The list returns deleted updates, so
clients show them as deleted rather than drop them.

**Links and metrics** are JSONB that only the service checks. Links are http
or https only, because the UI renders them as `href`s in the client's browser,
and the service keeps that check.

**Attachments.** Attachment bytes are served safely by
`GET /objects/{id}/content` (attachment, nosniff, sandboxed), but the ui reads
them into object URLs, which belong to the app's origin and keep the
uploader's content type. Every ui page that reads them goes through
`objectURLOf` (ui `src/services/exalynt/objects.ts`), which keeps only plain
images and videos renderable, or an uploaded SVG or HTML file opened in a tab
runs as the app. The portal will too, once it reads real updates.

**Who started a block** is `capacities.started_by`, which isn't always its
engineer: `Start` takes `capacity:manage` at team or global scope too. Blocks
started before migration 00088 have no `started_at`.

gaps.name: Impersonators can create lasting tokens
gaps.description: Someone impersonating a user through the sign-in provider can create a token for them, which outlasts the impersonation.

gaps.name: Bans can arrive late or out of order
gaps.description: A ban can arrive late or out of order: a banned user's tokens work until word of it arrives. An older update arriving after the ban undoes it until the next update or a sync, and nothing runs the sync on a schedule, so that could be a long time. An update that doesn't mention a ban leaves it alone.

gaps.name: Invitations never expire and can't be resent
gaps.description: Invitations never expire and can't be resent: an Admin revokes one and invites the same address again.

gaps.name: Sign-up reveals a team's contact details
gaps.description: Anyone who signs up sees the names and email addresses of the team they're given, with no one at Exalynt having looked at them first. Since anyone can create organizations, doing it again and again can show more than one team.

gaps.name: Closed organizations' data never deleted
gaps.description: Nothing of an organization's data is deleted after it closes, even on request.

gaps.name: No privacy notice at sign-up
gaps.description: Sign-up doesn't link to a privacy notice, and the agreements with the services that hold people's details (sign-in, email, monitoring) aren't confirmed.

gaps.name: Only one scope per permission
gaps.description: A permission can be given only one scope when editing a role, though several are allowed. Saving a role's permissions keeps only the widest, so own and team becomes team, and someone on no team loses their own reach. That happens when a role with a permission given several scopes is saved in the app.

gaps.name: Deploys restore built-in roles
gaps.description: Each deploy puts back permissions taken off Admin, Member, Billing, and Administrator, and renaming one makes a new role under the old name. A role says so going by name alone, so a role of the other kind with one of those names says it too. That bites when an admin takes a permission off a built-in role, or renames one.

gaps.name: No preview before sending an Engineer Agreement
gaps.description: An admin has no preview of an Engineer Agreement before sending it, the terms they choose from are a copy of the real catalog, and the list of engineers doesn't say whose agreements are in effect.

gaps.name: New versions not offered to organizations
gaps.description: A new version of the Client Agreement isn't offered to an organization that accepted an earlier one, and nothing sends a client new terms (it has none). That matters once a new version of the Client Agreement is published.

gaps.name: Names outside Western alphabets lost in PDFs
gaps.description: A name with characters outside Western European alphabets shows them as "?" in the PDF, and the PDF keeps them that way once accepted.

gaps.name: Version 1 changed in place after acceptance
gaps.description: The definition of Fulfilled, and version 1 of the Client Agreement, were changed in place to say the engineer marks a block fulfilled and nobody reviews it: a copy accepted before then still says a block is fulfilled once it's reviewed and approved. Version 1 was changed in place again to stop saying each block is assigned to a product: a copy accepted before then still does.

gaps.name: New versions not offered to engineers
gaps.description: A new version of the Engineer Agreement isn't offered to an engineer who accepted an earlier one. That matters once a new version of the Engineer Agreement is published.

gaps.name: Names outside Western alphabets lost in PDFs
gaps.description: A name with characters outside Western European alphabets shows them as "?" in the PDF, and the PDF keeps them that way once accepted.

gaps.name: Version 1 changed in place after acceptance
gaps.description: The definition of Fulfilled, and version 1 of the Engineer Agreement, were changed in place to say the engineer marks a block fulfilled and nobody reviews it: a copy accepted before then still says a block is fulfilled once it's reviewed and approved.

gaps.name: Names outside Western alphabets lost in PDFs
gaps.description: A name with characters outside Western European alphabets shows them as "?" in the PDF, and the PDF keeps them that way once accepted.

gaps.name: Operations and infrastructure charges not shown
gaps.description: Clients can't see operations fees or infrastructure pass-through charges, each shown separately from capacity.

gaps.name: Charged purchases can go unrecorded
gaps.description: A purchase that was charged but not recorded has no invoice or blocks with Exalynt until it's retried, and the payment provider's updates about it are ignored, since Exalynt has no record of the invoice. If it can't be retried, it's sorted out by hand with the payment provider.

gaps.name: Unclear purchase retry safe only while open
gaps.description: If it can't be told whether a purchase went through, the client is told so, and trying again can't charge twice, but only while that attempt is still open. Closing it, or reloading, starts a new purchase.

gaps.name: Touch screens and screen readers untried
gaps.description: Real touch screens and screen readers haven't been tried. That matters for someone buying blocks on a touch screen or with a screen reader.

gaps.name: Engineers not told when taken off
gaps.description: An engineer isn't told when a client's move or unschedule takes them off a block, so a client can take an engineer off by moving a block away and back. My Schedule shows it the next time it's read.

gaps.name: Clients not told of stranded blocks
gaps.description: When a claim leaves another block with nobody who can take it, that block's client isn't told, and it surfaces as a missed week an admin rebooks.

gaps.name: Clicking a block unclaims it
gaps.description: Before a block's week starts, clicking it on My Schedule unclaims it, so an engineer can't open its page from there until the week starts.

gaps.name: Stream messages can't be edited or deleted
gaps.description: With Stream, nobody can edit or delete a message once it's sent. That matters when someone sends a message they need to take back.

gaps.name: Space membership changes never retried
gaps.description: Nothing is retried. If the messaging provider fails to put someone in a space, such as an engineer who just joined a client's team, they're asked to request access when they open its conversations, until a conversation is next started for that client, which puts everyone who belongs in the space. If it fails to take someone out, such as an engineer who left the team, they stay in the space and can keep reading it until they're taken out by hand. Starting a conversation says when it failed, and can be tried again.

gaps.name: PDF leaves out each focus's planned pace
gaps.description: The PDF offers the project on each pace as an option, with every focus on it, and leaves out the pace each focus was planned on.

gaps.name: Departed engineers' blocks can't be fulfilled
gaps.description: Only a block's own engineer can mark it fulfilled, so a block whose engineer has left can't be fulfilled by anyone else.

gaps.name: No moving blocks in the admin app
gaps.description: An admin has no way to move a block in the admin app yet.

gaps.name: Moving a block drops its engineer
gaps.description: Moving a block always takes its engineer off. Whoever moves it, it's to keep its engineer if they can fit it in the new week, and only otherwise go back to the shared queue for that week.

gaps.name: Room counts the whole team's availability
gaps.description: A week has room when the team's combined availability covers a block, though capacity a client buys is never split across engineers, so it's to need one eligible engineer who can fit the whole block alone. An admin sorts out a block no single engineer can fit. That shows when no single eligible engineer can fit a block into a week the team has room in.

gaps.name: Team changes can overbook a week
gaps.description: Team changes aren't checked against bookings, so a week can end up overbooked after it was booked. The admin's overview flags it only across all of Exalynt, not per team, and nothing else happens. An engineer offering less takes blocks out instead.

gaps.name: Clients not told of unscheduled blocks
gaps.description: A client isn't told when an engineer's reduction unschedules one of their blocks. It's back among the blocks they have to schedule.

gaps.name: Assignments not checked for eligibility
gaps.description: An admin putting an engineer on a block isn't checked for that engineer's eligibility. That matters when an admin puts an engineer on a block of a client their team doesn't support.

gaps.name: Assignments not checked for availability
gaps.description: An admin putting an engineer on a block isn't checked for that engineer's availability. That matters when an admin puts an engineer on a block they don't have the availability for.

gaps.name: Team names can name clients
gaps.description: Nothing checks that a team's name doesn't name one of its clients, though every client it supports sees it. Name teams for what they do. That matters if a team is named after one of its clients.

gaps.name: Terms from the app's own catalog copy
gaps.description: The terms on an invitation come from the app's own copy of the terms catalog. That matters once the terms catalog changes and the app's copy isn't updated.

gaps.name: Invitations don't expire
gaps.description: An engineer invitation doesn't expire. That matters if an old invitation is accepted by someone who shouldn't join any more.

gaps.name: Existing clients spotted by name only
gaps.description: A company that's already a client can only be spotted by having the same name, so one signing up under another name counts as new.

gaps.name: Email law not reviewed, and no opt-out
gaps.description: What the law asks of email a partner has Exalynt send to someone who never asked for it, such as a way to opt out, hasn't been reviewed, and the invitation has no opt-out.

gaps.name: Moving a client loses its history
gaps.description: Moving a client starts its "since" afresh, and nothing keeps the partnerships a client was attributed to before. That happens when Exalynt moves a client to another partnership.

gaps.name: Phones hide client source and earning window
gaps.description: On a phone, how each client came and its earning window aren't shown.

gaps.name: Existing clients spotted by name only
gaps.description: A company that's already a client can only be spotted by having the same name, so one signing up under another name counts as new.

gaps.name: No handover or new terms for partnerships
gaps.description: Nothing hands a partnership to another manager, or sends it new terms. That matters once a partnership needs a new manager or new terms.

gaps.name: Upcoming lead and support shares can change
gaps.description: Upcoming lead and support earnings follow today's team and availability, so they can change before the block is fulfilled. Who earns them is fixed when it's fulfilled, and the basis and percentages aren't fixed when the block is assigned.

gaps.name: Expected pay not shown on the block
gaps.description: What an assigned block will pay shows only among a person's earnings, not on the block.

gaps.name: Earnings lost when a user is deleted
gaps.description: Someone's earnings go if their user is deleted.

gaps.name: One account, its country fixed once chosen
gaps.description: There's one account per person or partnership, and its country is fixed once it's chosen, as the payments partner's form holds one and verifies them for one country. That matters for someone who wants a second account, or to be paid in another country.

gaps.name: No payouts to Mexico
gaps.description: People can't be paid in Mexico, so it isn't offered as a country: the payments partner can't send there.

gaps.name: Form asks for business details
gaps.description: The payments partner's form asks for business details, as if the payee sold something: a website or a description of what they sell, even in the US, and more of them outside it. In Canada it also asks for an ID document and a selfie.

gaps.name: Changes need the payments partner's dashboard
gaps.description: Once an account is set up, changing it happens in the payments partner's own dashboard rather than its form.

gaps.name: Removing an account means starting over
gaps.description: Removing an account closes it with the payments partner, so adding one again means going through their checks from the start.

gaps.name: Nothing can be held back from a release
gaps.description: Nothing can be held back from a release, or looked into from it. That matters when an admin wants to hold back or look into one payee's payout before a release.

gaps.name: No release notes for the API or apps
gaps.description: Nothing tells people what changed in a release, for the API or the apps, Beta features included. Changes show only in the reference and in git history.

gaps.name: Leaving out the organization runs on platform
gaps.description: `X-Organization-ID` is optional, so anyone signed in can leave it out and run on `api_platform`. Holding no platform role, they hold no permissions and `authz.Require` refuses them, so nothing crosses today, but Bounds are all that stand in the way. That matters if a query reachable without an organization forgets its Bounds.

gaps.name: Shared tables lack row-level security
gaps.description: Shared tables have no row-level security, `users` above all, as staff names appear across organizations: a query there that forgets to filter can read every user's name and email.

gaps.name: User sync doesn't remove people from spaces
gaps.description: `api sync users` has no hook, so a ban or deletion it applies doesn't take the user out of the provider's spaces. That matters when it bans or deletes someone in a real messaging provider's spaces.

tradeoffs.name: Tokens have no scopes
tradeoffs.description: A token can do everything its user can, wherever it works: there are no scopes.
tradeoffs.drawback: A script that needs only a little access holds all of its user's. That matters when a script's token leaks or the script misbehaves.

tradeoffs.name: Managing tokens needs a session, not a token
tradeoffs.description: Managing tokens needs a session: a token can't list, create, or revoke tokens.
tradeoffs.drawback: Tokens can't be managed from scripts.

tradeoffs.name: Limited tokens still reach their user's record
tradeoffs.description: A limited token still reaches its user's own record: it can read and change their profile, including updating it from the sign-in provider, and sees their platform role and applications.
tradeoffs.drawback: A limited token reaches more than its organizations, though none of it reveals another organization. That matters only when a limited token leaks or its script misbehaves.

tradeoffs.name: Limited tokens can leave an organization
tradeoffs.description: A limited token can remove its user from one of its organizations, as their own session can.
tradeoffs.drawback: A script can take its user out of an organization. That's within its limit, and acts on nothing else. It matters only if a script actually does.

tradeoffs.name: Failed authentication isn't rate limited
tradeoffs.description: Requests that fail to authenticate aren't rate limited.
tradeoffs.drawback: Each request with a bad token costs a lookup that nothing counts, though a token can't be guessed. That matters only if someone floods the API with bad tokens.

tradeoffs.name: No client email on scheduling or availability
tradeoffs.description: Clients aren't emailed when a block is scheduled, or when an availability change affects their capacity: the client scheduled the block themselves, and an availability change that matters reaches them as a moved preferred week.
tradeoffs.drawback: A client hears nothing of a scheduled block, nor of an availability change that doesn't move a preferred week.

tradeoffs.name: One set of choices for all organizations
tradeoffs.description: One set of choices covers every organization someone belongs to, and each notification is to name the one it's about.
tradeoffs.drawback: Someone in several organizations can't choose differently for each.

tradeoffs.name: Last channel can't be removed
tradeoffs.description: The last channel can't be removed, as what's always on needs somewhere to go. Being always on means at least one channel, not all of them.
tradeoffs.drawback: Nobody can remove every channel to stop notifications altogether.

tradeoffs.name: Closing the account by email
tradeoffs.description: Closing the account is a conversation with Exalynt, by email from the Organization page.
tradeoffs.drawback: Nothing in the portal starts or tracks closing, and the organization isn't deleted afterwards.

tradeoffs.name: Fifty invitations a day
tradeoffs.description: An organization, and each person, can send 50 invitations a day.
tradeoffs.drawback: An organization inviting more people than that waits until the next day.

tradeoffs.name: Last save wins on names and roles
tradeoffs.description: The last save wins on the organization's name and on member roles: nothing checks what the person last read.
tradeoffs.drawback: Two people changing the same thing at once can undo each other's change without knowing. That takes two people changing the organization's name, or the same member's role, at once.

tradeoffs.name: Member managers can give any role
tradeoffs.description: Whoever can manage members can give anyone any role, Admin included.
tradeoffs.drawback: A role that manages members can do everything. That matters when someone is given a role that manages members but isn't meant to do everything.

tradeoffs.name: Agreements visible to every member
tradeoffs.description: Every member of an organization sees its agreements, whatever their role.
tradeoffs.drawback: Members and Billing see the organization's terms with Exalynt, not just its Admins.

tradeoffs.name: Prices listed before tax
tradeoffs.description: Prices are listed before tax everywhere, such as on estimates and when choosing blocks.
tradeoffs.drawback: The tax is only known once an order is reviewed, since the payment provider works it out from the billing address.

tradeoffs.name: Client members not shown to staff
tradeoffs.description: A client's members aren't shown, since staff can't see them.
tradeoffs.drawback: There's no primary contact for a client.

tradeoffs.name: Block status, not the work done
tradeoffs.description: A block shows who's on it and where it stands, not what was done on it.
tradeoffs.drawback: A client can't tell from home what was done on a block, and opens the block's own page for that.

tradeoffs.name: Gravatar as the fallback photo on Stream
tradeoffs.description: With Stream, someone without an uploaded photo shows their Gravatar, as they do everywhere else in the app.
tradeoffs.drawback: Stream keeps a link made from a hash of their email address. That's only while Stream is the messaging provider.

tradeoffs.name: Written for administrators, not narrower roles
tradeoffs.description: It's written for administrators: without full reads of people, teams, capacity and clients the list doesn't load, and with narrower reach it shows only what that reaches.
tradeoffs.drawback: There's no rule for what a team-limited view of people shows, as only the admin view matters for now. That matters once someone other than an administrator needs the list of people.

tradeoffs.name: Last save wins, without a warning
tradeoffs.description: When two people edit one estimate at once, the later save replaces the earlier one, without a warning.
tradeoffs.drawback: The earlier person's changes are lost without them knowing. That takes two people editing one estimate at once.

tradeoffs.name: Deleting an estimate is permanent
tradeoffs.description: Deleting an estimate is permanent.
tradeoffs.drawback: Getting one back means restoring a backup. That matters when someone deletes an estimate by mistake.

tradeoffs.name: Fulfilled is final, no reopening
tradeoffs.description: Marking a block fulfilled is final.
tradeoffs.drawback: A fulfilled block can't be reopened, even when it was marked fulfilled by mistake.

tradeoffs.name: Names unique across teams, not per client
tradeoffs.description: Team names are unique across all teams, not per client.
tradeoffs.drawback: Two teams can't both be called "Platform", even for different clients.

tradeoffs.name: Revoking leaves the emailed link working
tradeoffs.description: Revoking an invitation doesn't stop its link: the email still has the link with the partnership's referral code.
tradeoffs.drawback: Whoever uses a revoked invitation's link is still attributed to the partnership.

tradeoffs.name: Earnings start from launch, not backdated
tradeoffs.description: Partnerships earn only on blocks fulfilled since partnership earnings existed.
tradeoffs.drawback: Blocks fulfilled before partnership earnings existed earn the partnership nothing.

tradeoffs.name: Earlier blocks count only after attribution
tradeoffs.description: Blocks a client bought before this was built count as bought for the partnership only if they were bought after the client was attributed to it.
tradeoffs.drawback: Blocks bought before the client was attributed earn the partnership nothing.

tradeoffs.name: Each partnership has its own account
tradeoffs.description: Each partnership has its own payout account, even when several are paid to the same bank account.
tradeoffs.drawback: Someone managing several partnerships that are paid to the same bank account sets it up, and goes through the payments partner's checks, on each.

tradeoffs.name: One country per account, fixed once chosen
tradeoffs.description: There's one account per partnership, and its country is fixed once it's chosen, as the payments partner's form holds one and verifies it for one country.
tradeoffs.drawback: A partnership can't be paid to a second account, or move its account to another country. That matters when a partnership wants a second account, or to be paid in another country.

tradeoffs.name: Mexico not offered as a country
tradeoffs.description: Mexico isn't offered as a country, since the payments partner can't send there.
tradeoffs.drawback: Partnerships can't be paid in Mexico.

tradeoffs.name: Payments partner's form used as it is
tradeoffs.description: Accounts are set up on the payments partner's form as it is.
tradeoffs.drawback: The form asks for business details, as if the partnership sold something: a website or a description of what it sells, and more of them outside the US. In Canada it also asks for an ID document and a selfie.

tradeoffs.name: Changes made in the payments partner's dashboard
tradeoffs.description: Once an account is set up, changing it happens in the payments partner's own dashboard rather than its form.
tradeoffs.drawback: Managers change the bank account somewhere other than where they set it up.

tradeoffs.name: Removing an account closes it
tradeoffs.description: Removing an account closes it with the payments partner.
tradeoffs.drawback: Adding one again means going through their checks from the start. That matters only for a manager who removes the account and later adds one again.

tradeoffs.name: Pre-production payouts left saying Paid
tradeoffs.description: Payouts released before production sent money through the payments partner are left saying Paid.
tradeoffs.drawback: They say Paid, though nothing was sent.

tradeoffs.name: Paid means in the balance, not the bank
tradeoffs.description: Paid means the money has reached the partnership's balance with the payments partner, not its bank.
tradeoffs.drawback: The payments partner pays it on to the bank itself, usually within a couple of days.

tradeoffs.name: Application access enforced only by the front ends
tradeoffs.description: Which applications someone is offered is `application_access`, held per user and not by role, and only the front ends act on it: they decide what to show by it, and the API keeps checking permissions.
tradeoffs.drawback: Someone who isn't offered an application can still call its routes with whatever their permissions allow. That matters when an organization counts on application access alone to keep someone out of an application.

tradeoffs.name: Tenant set per transaction, not per connection
tradeoffs.description: The organization or partnership is set with `SET LOCAL` in a transaction around each statement, a `UnitOfWork`'s or a short one of its own, rather than on a connection kept for the request.
tradeoffs.drawback: A statement outside a `UnitOfWork` costs three more round trips, so work issuing many belongs in one.

tradeoffs.name: Agreements enforced in the apps, not the API
tradeoffs.description: The apps hold people to an agreement, not the API: the portal's, console's and hub's gates keep someone out until one is in effect, and the API answers what their role allows regardless.
tradeoffs.drawback: Someone using the API directly can still do what their role allows without an agreement in effect.

tradeoffs.name: PDFs drawn in Go without Unicode fonts
tradeoffs.description: The PDF is laid out in Go with fpdf's Helvetica, not a browser or a Unicode font, so there's no headless browser to run or font to ship.
tradeoffs.drawback: A character outside Windows-1252 is "?" for good once accepted, so a name with characters outside Western European alphabets keeps them as "?" in its PDF.

tradeoffs.name: Accepted agreements kept after their user is deleted
tradeoffs.description: Accepted agreements outlive their user: deleting a user clears `user_id` on their accepted ones (migration 91) and keeps their PDFs, since the PDF is the record of what was agreed.
tradeoffs.drawback: A deleted person's name and email stay in those PDFs and rows. That matters when a user who accepted an agreement is deleted.

tradeoffs.name: Recurrence rules kept, not a weeks column
tradeoffs.description: Availability is stored as recurrence rules, not a `weeks` column. A column would do, as the rules are only ever `FREQ=WEEKLY` with an optional `COUNT`, but moving off them is an expand/contract migration on a table Capacity reads, with nothing to gain for now.
tradeoffs.drawback: The database can't filter by the weeks a rule covers, so `from` on the overrides list is widened by 51 weeks and checked in Go, and a page of overrides can come back short.

tradeoffs.name: Payment provider is the source of truth
tradeoffs.description: The provider is the source of truth for invoices and billing details, and our row only links to it: we keep the least needed to find an invoice and relate its blocks.
tradeoffs.drawback: Reading an invoice is a call to the provider, and a provider without hosted pages doesn't fit.

tradeoffs.name: Tax handled by the payments provider, not its own
tradeoffs.description: Tax is part of the payments provider, not a provider of its own: the provider already holds the billing address tax is worked out from, and issues the invoice the tax goes on, so a separate tax provider would pull billing details out of it and push tax lines back in.
tradeoffs.drawback: A payments provider that can't work out tax has to call a tax service inside its own implementation. That matters only if a payments provider that can't work out tax is added.

tradeoffs.name: Week's room combined, not per engineer
tradeoffs.description: A week's room is combined, not per engineer: a block fits if the total covers it, even if no one engineer could do it alone, as the preferred week is a target and not a guarantee.
tradeoffs.drawback: A block can be scheduled into a week where no single engineer can fit it, and an admin sorts it out.

tradeoffs.name: Prices copied onto the estimate when made
tradeoffs.description: Prices are copied onto the estimate when it's made, so a client's estimate doesn't change when prices do. Every response returns the copy as `capacity_prices`, and the console and portal price from it.
tradeoffs.drawback: A capacity type added later only reaches estimates made after it's recorded.

tradeoffs.name: Unindexed ILIKE search over estimates
tradeoffs.description: Search is `ILIKE '%word%'` over four columns, with no index: at 2,000 estimates that's a few milliseconds, measured against the local stack on 2026-10-23.
tradeoffs.drawback: It scans, which matters only once estimates grow far beyond the 2,000 measured.

tradeoffs.name: Lists returned whole, not paged
tradeoffs.description: Members, invitations, and `GET /v1/clients` are returned whole, not paged: an organization is sized for tens of members and Exalynt for tens to hundreds of clients.
tradeoffs.drawback: The last-manager check reads every member and organization role on each removal and role change. That gets slow only once an organization grows well beyond tens of members.

tradeoffs.name: Invitation routes shared, with stable copies beside
tradeoffs.description: `GET /invitations` and `POST /invitations/{id}/accept` stay shared, with stable organization-only copies beside them: they also serve invitations to work with Exalynt and to manage a partnership, whose shape is still settling, so the stable contract for organizations is `/users/me/organization-invitations`.
tradeoffs.drawback: There are two ways to list and accept an organization's invitation, and onboarding reads both listings.

tradeoffs.name: Sending limits counted from invitation rows
tradeoffs.description: Sending limits are counted from the invitations themselves, not a limiter or a log of sends: the day's new invitations are a count of `client_invitations` rows created in the last 24 hours, revoked ones included, and a resend compares the row's `sent_at`, so nothing else is stored or run. That's why revoking sets `revoked_at` and blanks the address rather than deleting (migration 95): a deleted row would free up a slot, and the count needs no address.
tradeoffs.drawback: Two invitations at the same moment can both pass the 50th, and the count is a rolling 24 hours, not a calendar day. That matters only when a partnership reaches the day's limit of 50 invitations.

tradeoffs.name: Waiting payouts worked out on read, not stored
tradeoffs.description: What's waiting is worked out on read, not stored as a run: there's no scheduler or draft to keep in step, and a week nobody released rolls into the next.
tradeoffs.drawback: Every read asks the provider about each payee's account. That gets slower as the number of payees grows.

qualities.name: Utility
qualities.question: Is it worth building, and is this the right way to build it?
qualities.why: It's worth building, and this is the right way to build it.

levels.summary: Just enough for someone to judge the idea.

outcomes.text: Those judging the idea can try it, or watch it run, enough to tell whether it's worth doing and whether this is the way to do it.

implementation.text: The question it's meant to answer written down before it's built, and the answer once it's judged.
A clickable UI with fake or hard-coded data.
Two or three versions of the key screen, to choose between.
A stub endpoint or command that returns realistic output, or a mock server from a draft API description.
One run by hand on a recent day's records, with its output shown next to the source.
A draft of the main calls and the config format, tried by one team that would use it, in a branch of their code.
A script or notebook that runs the core idea on made-up or sample data.
A spike against the one real integration the idea depends on, when that's the open question.
A dry run, a sandbox, or a test account when trying it would otherwise change a real system or reach real people.

overengineering.text: Polishing anything the idea doesn't depend on.
Building out the parts of the system that aren't the question.
Packaging an installed app when a script on sample files answers the question.
A production-like environment, infrastructure as code, or a deploy pipeline, when a local run or one preview lets people try it.
Sending real emails or texts when the question is the workflow, and showing the message on screen would answer it.
Putting it on a schedule, when running it by hand answers the question.
Building for several platforms, such as both iOS and Android, when one answers the question.

levels.summary: Real use on the real system, to learn what it should become.

outcomes.text: It works end to end on the real system.

implementation.text: Wired to real storage and services, with sample data where real data isn't needed.
