Installed the way its users will get it, from a packaged build or the real registry, not run from source.

outcomes.text: It's used for real.

implementation.text: A few people, teams, or systems using it for real work, or a job running on a real schedule.
A pilot with one client or team doing real work, with their usual way of working kept as a fallback.
Run alongside what it replaces, on real input, with the results compared before anything acts on them, when a wrong result would cost money or reach customers.
Each consuming service keeps its old calculation and chooses between the two, so it can go back without a release.
Whether it's being used, and how, is known, such as from its logs or by asking those using it.

overengineering.text: Usage tracking built into what people install.

outcomes.text: What's learned from using it shapes what comes next.

implementation.text: Notes on what worked and what didn't, feeding the next round of changes.

overengineering.text: Settling its shape. Big changes are still expected.

levels.summary: Confidence that the need is real and the approach is right. From here, it's refinement.

outcomes.text: The need and the solution are confirmed, so what changes from here is refinement.

implementation.text: Feedback is about details, not direction.
Those integrating have run their real flows through it without needing a change to its shape.

outcomes.text: What success looks like is agreed.

implementation.text: Success measures agreed with whoever asked for it, such as adoption, time saved, error rates, or jobs completed.
Today's numbers measured before it's widely used, such as the current no-show rate, so there's something to compare with.
Use measured from the services it calls, such as requests by its version, not from people's devices.

overengineering.text: Analytics built into what people install, when asking them or counting what it produces would do.

levels.summary: Proof, from real use, that it delivers what it's for.

outcomes.text: It's shown to deliver what it's for in real use.

implementation.text: When it's too early to show, such as for a yearly workflow, a known gap with the date it will be shown by.
Usage or outcome numbers that meet the measures agreed at Beta.
The systems it was built for rely on it, and the copies of the logic it replaced are retired.

overengineering.text: An analytics pipeline built only to prove value, when the numbers can come from its own data or the client's reports.

qualities.name: Usability
qualities.question: Can its users learn and use it on their own?
qualities.why: Its users, people or programs, can learn it, use it, and recover from mistakes on their own.

implementation.text: Whoever built it walks those trying it through it.
Shown on the device those judging it will really use, such as a front-desk tablet or a phone.
A request collection or a few curl commands for the main calls.

overengineering.text: User docs, or polishing flows beyond what trying the idea needs.
Layouts for every screen size, when those judging it use one device.

Handling edge cases or bad input, unless they're the question.

levels.summary: The main path is checked, so a change can't quietly break it.

outcomes.text: The main path is known to work after every change.

outcomes.text: Errors are visible, never silent.

implementation.text: Input validated where it enters.
Records or files it can't process rejected with the reason, or counted and logged, never dropped quietly or partly imported without saying so.
A failed call to an outside service, such as a message that didn't send, recorded where someone can see it.
A run that fails ends as a failure the scheduler can see, never a success with nothing written.
Every failure ends with a non-zero exit code, including one reported by a service it called.
Failures return an error status, never a 200 with the error inside.

levels.summary: Edge cases and errors are handled, and checked too.

outcomes.text: Unusual input and error paths are handled correctly.

implementation.text: Data validated before it's written.
Empty, missing, duplicate, and oversized input handled.
A repeated request or redelivered message doesn't do its work twice, such as with an idempotency key or a duplicate check, when doing it twice would create a second record or send a second message.
Two people changing the same thing at once can't both succeed unnoticed, such as with a unique constraint or a version check, where that would double-book or overwrite someone's work.
Numbers kept exact where exactness matters, such as money in integer minor units or a decimal type.
A rule for when the same item changes on the device and elsewhere before it syncs, and the person told when their change didn't win.
Records that fail validation set aside with the reason, and records changed at the source after loading updated, not added again.
Events it sends carry a unique ID and a timestamp, so receivers can drop duplicates and put them in order.
A malformed or incomplete config reported with the file, line, and key at fault, before anything is changed.

outcomes.text: How it handles unusual input and errors is known to keep working as it changes.

implementation.text: Made-up, hard-coded, or in-memory data, local files of made-up data, or a throwaway database.

Resuming or undoing an operation that fails partway.

Failing over to a second provider.

Cells that could run as formulas escaped in exported spreadsheets.

overengineering.text: A self-update mechanism of its own, when a package manager installs and updates it.

A third party or client system with no stated level judged by what it promises, such as a preview label, a deprecation policy, or a support agreement.
A widely used package that stays at 0.x judged by how it's maintained and how it changes, not by its version number.
Endpoints or services still being built alongside it counted as early, and written down as a known gap until they settle.

levels.summary: Protected against misuse, and follows the rules that apply.

outcomes.text: It's protected against misuse at the level it's exposed.

implementation.text: Rate limits and input size limits.
Protection against cross-site request forgery.
Sign-in attempts limited, session cookies secure and HTTP-only, and sessions that expire.
The checks in OWASP ASVS level 1.
The OWASP API Security Top 10 checked, such as object-level authorization and mass assignment.
What it receives is checked for who sent it, such as signed webhooks.
Webhooks it sends are signed.
API keys that can be rotated and revoked.
Only its own services can put work on its queue, and a message can trigger only what it's for.
Links sent in messages use unguessable tokens that expire, and open only what they're for.
A lost or stolen device can't be used to reach the data, through the platform's storage protection and sessions that can be revoked.
Windows reach the system only through a few named calls, such as an Electron preload script, each checking its arguments, under a content security policy.
Signed releases, so the platform or package manager can verify them.
Known vulnerabilities in dependencies found and fixed.

overengineering.text: A web application firewall, bot detection, or a bug bounty, before its exposure or a real incident calls for one.
OAuth, mutual TLS, or request signing for callers when keys over TLS are enough and nobody asks for more.
Encrypting local data with a key of its own, when disk encryption and the OS account already protect it and no duty asks for more.
Certificate pinning, jailbreak detection, or code obfuscation without a specific threat that calls for them.
Sessions so short that people have to sign in again while offline.
Rate limiting inside the tool, when the service it calls enforces its own limits.

outcomes.text: The legal and regulatory duties that apply to it are known and met.

implementation.text: Privacy duties met, such as exporting or deleting someone's personal data on request, with a deletion at the source reaching the copies it made.

Rates and rules carry the dates they take effect, so a change in the law ships before it applies.
Rules about where data may be stored, and for how long.
Consent and opt-out for the messages it sends, such as honoring STOP replies, where the law requires them. Transactional messages, such as order confirmations, often don't need an opt-out.
An audit log where a law requires one, such as for health records.
Where data stays on people's devices, how long it's kept, and how it's deleted written down, so the client can meet its own duties.
The app stores' privacy details match what it collects.
The source of each rule it implements, such as a law or regulation, recorded next to the rule.

overengineering.text: A certification, such as SOC 2 or HITRUST, before a client or law requires one.

outcomes.text: Personal data is collected only where it's needed.

implementation.text: Only the fields the work needs, with nothing kept just in case.
Functions and APIs take only what they need, such as a postal code instead of a whole customer record.
Personal data kept out of logs, error reports, crash reports, and analytics.
Error messages and debug output name what's wrong without repeating the personal data passed in.
Emails, texts, notifications, and webhooks carry no more personal data than they need.
Third-party services sent only what they need to do their part.
Copies it makes, such as reporting tables or exports, carry only the fields their readers need.
Location and other metadata removed from photos and files, unless the work needs them.
Device permissions, such as the camera or location, asked for only when a feature needs them.
The legal duties that come with it, such as consent, or an agreement with a provider that processes it, in place before the first real personal data arrives.

outcomes.text: Its dependencies are maintained, and licensed for how it's used.

implementation.text: Licenses checked when a dependency is added, against how it's distributed, such as copyleft code in an app-store app.
Dependency versions pinned, such as with a lock file.
A lock file published with it, such as `npm-shrinkwrap.json`, or a bundled build, so people install the versions that were tested.

A supported Electron release, since older ones stop getting security fixes.

overengineering.text: Security reviews, compliance audits.

levels.summary: Its sensitive parts are reviewed, and actions can be traced.

outcomes.text: Its handling of credentials, payments, personal data, and permissions is known to be sound.

implementation.text: A security review of sign-in and permission checks.
The checks in OWASP ASVS level 2.
The checks in OWASP MASVS that fit its risk, such as for storage, network, and authentication.
A review of how it gets, stores, sends, and refreshes tokens, including what debug output shows.
A review of what its windows can ask the rest of the app to do, and of how updates are checked before they install.
A review of how API keys are issued, rotated, and revoked.
Data and logs kept no longer than they're needed, backups included.
Builds that can be traced to their source, with a list of what's in them, such as SLSA provenance and an SBOM, where others install or build on it.

A penetration test, where the risk warrants one.

Root and jailbreak detection, obfuscation, or anti-tampering beyond what the client's risk calls for.

outcomes.text: Each part has only the access it needs.

implementation.text: Where a service offers no narrower token, a separate revocable token for each pipeline, with the missing scopes written down as a gap in that service.
Service accounts and tokens limited to what each part needs.
People's access to production limited to those who operate it, and removed when they leave.
The app's database user can't change the schema, and migrations run as a separate one.
Read-only access to the systems it reads from, and write access only to its own tables.
The narrowest token scope each command needs, and a deploy-only token in CI.
A publish token that can publish only this package, kept in CI.
Only the device permissions it uses.

outcomes.text: Sensitive actions can be traced to who did them.

implementation.text: The sensitive actions agreed, such as changing permissions, exporting data, or moving money.
An audit log of sensitive actions.
Staff reaching a client's data, such as for support, logged and visible to that client.
Who created, rotated, or revoked each API key, or changed a webhook address, recorded.
Manual reruns, backfills, and replayed messages recorded with who started them.
Who's acting, such as the person or the CI run, sent with each sensitive call, so the service's audit log records it.
Who published each version, and from which commit, recorded.

overengineering.text: Logging every action, instead of the sensitive ones.
A separate tamper-proof audit store, when the client's duties don't call for one.
An audit log of its own on people's devices or inside a library, when the service it calls or the software using it records who did what.

qualities.name: Compatibility
qualities.question: Does it fit with what's around it?
qualities.why: It works with the systems, platforms, and standards around it, and doesn't break those depending on it as it changes.

levels.summary: Kept apart, so it can't affect anything people rely on.

outcomes.text: It reaches only those who chose to try it, and from Alpha, the people the client has agreed it can reach.

implementation.text: Behind a feature flag that's off by default.
Opt-in for invited people or systems.
Turned on per tenant, only for the tenants who agreed to try it.
A separate environment, or a preview deploy.
A preview endpoint, or an experimental command or flag.
An experimental module.

A separate build or channel, not the public download or its auto-update.
Emails, messages, and other effects that reach people sent only to an allowlist or a sandbox, or logged without personal data instead of sent.
At Alpha, real messages sent only to people the client has agreed it can reach, such as a pilot client's customers.
A setting that stops sending to real people, for one tenant or everyone, without a release.
Where managed devices block unsigned apps, shown on the builder's machine or a VM the client approves.
Writes to a system others use go to its test environment or a test account.
Output written to its own tables or schema, and messages read from its own queue or subscription, never one something else relies on.

A feature flag system for a new product nobody relies on yet.
A public store listing, screenshots, or preparing for public review while it reaches only testers.

Signing builds only to get past managed devices, while it can be shown another way.
Packaging for every install channel, when one is enough to try it.

implementation.text: The stability mark on what it adds.

outcomes.text: It can be removed without affecting anything people rely on.

implementation.text: Kept to its own code, data, and settings, so taking it out touches nothing else.
What it created in other systems, such as deployed services, records, or files in people's repos, listed or marked so it can be cleaned up.
Its own tables or columns, not changes to ones others read.
Reads from systems people rely on with a read-only account, in small batches or off-hours, and writes nothing back.
In an app people already have installed, behind a remote flag, with its data kept apart from what the rest of the app keeps.
Those trying it know where it keeps its data, and how to delete it.
New config keys optional, or in a section older versions ignore.
No new runtime dependencies, and no code that runs on import, in a package others already install.

A version field or migrations for its config file.

levels.summary: Breaking changes are fine, as long as those trying it hear about them.

outcomes.text: Those depending on it hear about changes.

Running old and new versions of an endpoint side by side.

A new version alongside the old one.

Installs and updates on the client's managed machines, such as without admin rights or through their proxy.

qualities.name: Observability
qualities.question: When something goes wrong, does someone find out and see why?
qualities.why: When something goes wrong, someone finds out and can see why.

implementation.text: Console output is enough.
Outbound calls and messages printed to the console without credentials or personal data, so those watching can see they happened.
Counts of what each run read, skipped, and wrote, printed at the end.

overengineering.text: Logging setup, error tracking, metrics.
Product analytics, when watching people try it answers the question.
Crash reporting or analytics SDKs, which bring consent and privacy-label duties with them.
A logging dependency or debug hooks in the package.

Logs that name the file, row, and step, not the values in it.
The tenant in every error log.
Each run logs when it started and finished, how many records it read, wrote, and skipped, and why it failed.
A request ID returned with every response.

Data-quality frameworks, lineage tools, or freshness monitors.

Crash reporting, with consent.

levels.summary: Anyone on the team can change it confidently.

outcomes.text: Another engineer can change it confidently without the author, and tell what a change will affect.

implementation.text: Names and structure that explain themselves, with comments only where the reason isn't obvious.
Dependencies between parts explicit, with no hidden coupling through shared state or globals.
Someone new to it can set it up and ship a small change from its docs alone.

outcomes.text: There's no dead code, untracked TODOs, or unexplained complexity.

implementation.text: Dead code, and flags left over from earlier levels, removed.

overengineering.text: Rewriting working code to a newer pattern just to make it look cleaner.

qualities.name: Supportability
qualities.question: Who's responsible, and where do people turn?
qualities.why: Someone is responsible for it, and those depending on it know where to turn and what to expect when it breaks.

implementation.text: Whoever is exploring the idea looks after it.
Feedback through the test track's own tools, or a message to whoever built it.

overengineering.text: Bug tracking, support.
An in-app feedback or bug-report form.

levels.summary: Someone owns it, and problems get written down.

outcomes.text: It has an owner who decides its direction.

implementation.text: A named person or team.

overengineering.text: Support commitments, on-call.

outcomes.text: Problems can be reported, and aren't lost.

implementation.text: Bugs recorded in the team's tracker.
Those trying it know where to report a problem.
Where to report a problem shown in `--help`, the README, the package's metadata, and with unexpected errors.
A Help menu item, or the test track's feedback tools, with the version filled in.

overengineering.text: A help desk or ticketing system for those trying it.

levels.summary: Known problems get fixed, and people can see them.

outcomes.text: Known problems are fixed as they're found.

implementation.text: Bugs triaged regularly.

overengineering.text: Support response times, on-call.

outcomes.text: Known problems are visible to those depending on it.

implementation.text: Known issues listed in the docs, the release notes, or its known gaps.

levels.summary: Long-term ownership, with clear ways to get help.

outcomes.text: The owner is responsible for it long term.

implementation.text: On-call, or someone to reach outside working hours, if it's critical enough.
Where failures outside working hours can wait, a check at the start of each day and a way to catch up, instead of on-call.
Reviews of serious incidents, so they're less likely to happen again.
Dependencies, runtime, and database kept on supported versions, and upgraded before their end of life.
Time planned for keeping up with each year's OS release and the stores' requirements, and for renewing signing certificates.
A support policy saying which versions get fixes, and for how long.

overengineering.text: Round-the-clock on-call for work nobody needs outside working hours.
Out-of-hours on-call for a nightly job whose output isn't read until morning, when a morning check and a rerun are enough.
On-call for a library, when its problems reach the team through its consumers during working hours.

outcomes.text: Those depending on it know where to get help, and what response to expect.

implementation.text: A support channel, with expected response times.
When it serves a client's own customers, which questions go to the client and which reach the team is clear.
A status page or announcement during an outage.
A notice to those who read its output when data is late or incomplete, and again when it's fixed.
A way to reach support from inside it, with the version and the diagnostics people choose to share.
A named contact at each team or system that integrates with it, so notices reach a person.

overengineering.text: A status page for software that keeps working when its services are down, or whose outages whoever runs those services announces.
A self-serve developer portal with sign-up and ticketing, for a handful of callers onboarded by hand.

outcomes.text: Someone other than the author can change and operate it.

implementation.text: More than one engineer able to work on it.
Where one engineer works alone, a handover note and shared access, so someone else could take over.
Building, signing, and publishing done by CI, with certificates, store accounts, and publish rights held by the client or team, not one person.
